description: The people who served the gods — Greek and Roman priesthoods, the Pythia at Delphi, and Roman divination.
content_html:
The Role of Priests and Priestesses in Greece

In ancient Greece, priests and priestesses were not a professional clergy in the modern sense. A hiereus (male priest) or hiereia (female priestess) served a specific deity at a specific sanctuary. The role was often hereditary within a family, or held for a fixed term, or even purchased in some cities. Priests were not moral or spiritual advisers — their function was primarily practical: maintaining the temple, supervising the cult statue, ensuring sacrifices were performed correctly, and managing the sacred property of the sanctuary.

Priestesses played an especially important role in the cults of female deities. The priestess of Athena Polias at Athens — one of the most prestigious religious offices in the Greek world — was responsible for the care of the ancient olive-wood image of Athena on the Acropolis, a statue believed to have fallen from the sky. Priestesses of Hera and Demeter also held significant civic status, and in several cults women wielded a degree of public religious authority that was otherwise largely unavailable to them in Greek civic life.

Key Fact

Greek priests and priestesses were ritual specialists, not spiritual counsellors or moral leaders. Their essential duties were temple maintenance, correct performance of sacrifices and oversight of the sanctuary’s sacred treasures. The term hiereus (priest) and hiereia (priestess) literally relates to what is hieros — sacred or holy.

The Mantis: Prophets and Seers

Alongside priests, Greek religious life included the mantis (seer or prophet). The mantis was a specialist in reading divine signs: the flight of birds, the movement of flames in a sacrifice, the appearance of livers and lungs. Seers accompanied Greek armies in the field — no general would begin a battle without a favourable sacrifice reading. The historian Thucydides records that the Athenian general Nicias was so dependent on his seer’s readings that his paralysis during the catastrophic Sicilian Expedition of 415–413 BC contributed to the disaster.

The Oracle at Delphi

The most famous oracle in the ancient world was the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi. The sanctuary at Delphi, set high on the slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece, was considered the omphalos — the navel of the world — where Apollo had slain the serpent Python. Cities, kings and private individuals travelled to consult Apollo’s voice at Delphi before important decisions: going to war, founding colonies, making new laws.

The oracle’s voice was the Pythia — a woman chosen from among the local people, who served as Apollo’s mouthpiece. To consult the oracle, a consultee first paid a fee and performed a preliminary sacrifice. They were then admitted to the inner sanctuary. The Pythia sat on a tripod seat above a fissure in the rock from which vapours were said to rise, inducing her trance-like state of divine inspiration. Her often ambiguous or cryptic utterances were then transmitted by the priests in verse. The most famous example of ambiguity was the response given to the Lydian king Croesus, who asked whether he should attack the Persians: Apollo’s answer was that if he crossed the river Halys, a great empire would be destroyed — which was true, though the empire destroyed was his own.

The ancient literary accounts describe the Pythia as entering an ecstatic or trance-like state, sometimes thrashing and foaming, before delivering her prophecy. Modern geological surveys of Delphi have identified intersecting fault lines beneath the sanctuary and chemical analysis has found traces of ethylene gas in the spring water — a substance that can induce hallucination in low concentrations. This has led some scholars to argue there was a genuine physical basis for the Pythia’s altered state. Others are more sceptical, noting that the accounts of violent ecstasy may be literary exaggeration and that the consultations were heavily controlled by the priests. The question of whether the Pythia was genuinely inspired or performing a religious role is a good example of the problem of using literary sources alongside archaeological evidence.

Roman Priesthoods

Roman religious authority was embedded in the structures of the state in a way that had no equivalent in Greece. The two most important priestly colleges in Republican and Imperial Rome were the pontifices and the augures. The pontifices were guardians of the religious calendar, the correct formulae for prayer and sacrifice, and the legal boundaries between sacred and secular space. Their head, the Pontifex Maximus, was one of the most powerful religious and political figures in Rome — a title later assumed by the emperors themselves. Augustus became Pontifex Maximus in 12 BC, combining supreme religious authority with supreme political power.

The augures were specialists in reading the auspices — the signs by which the gods communicated their approval or disapproval of proposed actions. No significant Roman undertaking — a battle, an election, the founding of a temple — could proceed without favourable auspices. The augur would observe a defined area of sky and report what birds appeared, in what direction, and in what numbers. An eagle flying to the right was a good omen; a raven on the left was bad. This system meant that the college of augurs had the theoretical power to veto any public action by declaring the auspices unfavourable.

Key Fact

Three key groups of Roman religious officials: (1) Pontifices — guardians of religious law and the calendar, headed by the Pontifex Maximus; (2) Augures — readers of the auspices (bird signs); (3) Haruspices — specialists in reading omens from entrails (Etruscan in origin). All three operated alongside the Vestal Virgins, who maintained Rome’s sacred flame.

The Vestal Virgins were Rome’s most celebrated priestesses, six in number, chosen between the ages of six and ten to serve Vesta — goddess of the hearth — for thirty years. Their primary duty was to maintain the sacred fire in the Aedes Vestae (Temple of Vesta) in the Roman Forum. If the fire went out, it was a terrible omen for Rome. Vestals received extraordinary privileges: they could own property, make wills and travel in public without a male guardian. Their person was legally inviolable — harming a Vestal was a capital offence. However, the penalty for breaking their vow of chastity was to be buried alive in a chamber underground. Their status illustrates the paradox of Roman women in religion: they could hold great public religious authority while being legally barred from political life.
exam_tip_html: Questions about priests often ask you to Explain their role or to Compare Greek and Roman religious officials. The crucial point is that priests in both cultures were ritual specialists, not moral or spiritual guides. Examiners reward students who distinguish between the different roles: the Greek hiereus/hiereia who served a specific god at a specific temple; the Greek mantis who accompanied armies to read omens; the Roman pontifices who policed religious law; and the Roman augures who read the auspices. For source-analysis questions about the Pythia, use specific details in the source (the tripod, the vapours, the ambiguous phrasing of the oracle) and explain what they show about the Greeks’ belief in direct communication with the gods. Over-narrating the story of Croesus without making an analytical point is the most common mistake here.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greek priests (hiereus / hiereia) were ritual specialists for specific cults, not moral leaders; the mantis was a separate specialist in reading divine signs accompanying armies and advising leaders.
  • The Pythia at Delphi was Apollo’s mouthpiece, consulting the god for cities, kings and individuals; her often ambiguous answers were interpreted by attending priests and had enormous political influence.
  • Roman religious officials were embedded in the state: the pontifices oversaw religious law, the augures read the auspices (bird signs), and the Vestal Virgins maintained Rome’s sacred hearth fire — with the Pontifex Maximus eventually becoming the title of the emperor himself.

practice_questions.text: Name the title given to the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracular responses.
Describe the role of the augures in Roman religion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the augures were responsible for reading the auspices; they interpreted signs from the behaviour and flight of birds; they observed a defined area of sky; they reported whether the gods approved or disapproved of a proposed action; they could in theory veto any public action by declaring the auspices unfavourable; no significant Roman undertaking could proceed without their approval.

practice_questions.text: Read this account of the Oracle at Delphi: a woman known as the Pythia sat on a bronze tripod seat placed over a crack in the rock; below her, sweet-smelling vapours rose from underground; after consulting with those who had come from across the Greek world, she would fall into a state of divine inspiration and speak words that the attending priests recorded for the petitioner to take away. What does this description suggest about ancient Greek beliefs regarding communication with the gods? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Precise reference to specific details (tripod seat, crack in rock, vapours, state of divine inspiration, priests recording) with sustained analysis of what each implies about Greek religious belief (gods communicated directly with mortals; physical world could be a conduit for divine speech; the need for specialist intermediaries; the institutional framework around a single inspired woman); a clear judgement about what the combination reveals about Greek attitudes to divine communication.
Secure (3-4): Two or three details used with clear explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description without engaging with source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pontifices were so important in Roman religious and political life.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following developed points: they oversaw religious law and the calendar, giving them control over when public activities could take place; they guarded the correct formulae for prayer and sacrifice, making all public ritual dependent on their knowledge; their head (Pontifex Maximus) was one of the most powerful figures in Rome; Augustus took the title in 12 BC, combining religious and imperial authority; they defined the boundary between sacred and secular space, so any building project in Rome required their approval.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Oracle at Delphi was the most important religious institution in ancient Greece? Use named sources and a balanced argument in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained balanced argument weighing Delphi's importance (consulted before wars and colonial foundations, panhellenic authority, the famous Croesus story, the sanctuary's physical magnificence, accumulation of dedications from across Greece) against other institutions (the Olympic sanctuary, the Eleusinian Mysteries, civic priesthoods); different criteria of importance considered (political influence, numbers of worshippers, reach across the Greek world); evidence from named sources; clear supported judgement.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument with evidence for and against; some comparison; conclusion.
Developing (3-5): Points about Delphi but limited comparison or source use.
Emerging (1-2): Descriptive account; little argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Greek and Roman approaches to divination and reading divine signs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Greek mantis was an independent specialist accompanying armies vs Roman augures who were a formally constituted college of the state; the Pythia at Delphi offered personal consultations vs Roman auspices which governed all public business; Greek oracle ambiguous and interpreted by poets vs Roman auspicia highly codified with standardised rules for birds and directions) with named evidence for each and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about each culture.
Secure (3-4): Two differences explained with some evidence.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the role of the hiereia in ancient Greece?
options: A female specialist who read the entrails of sacrificed animals
A female priestess who served a specific deity and performed cult rituals
A prophetess who read the flight of birds for military commanders
A woman who maintained the sacred fire in the Temple of Vesta

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Roman augures specialise in?
options: Examining the livers of sacrificed animals
Maintaining the sacred fire of Vesta
Interpreting the will of the gods from the flight and behaviour of birds
Performing the preliminary sacrifices before major ceremonies

knowledge_checks.q: The head of the college of pontifices in Rome was called the _____.
The Pythia delivered her oracular responses while seated on a tripod above a fissure at the sanctuary of Apollo at _____.
Match each religious specialist to their role:
right: Greek seer who read omens and accompanied armies into battle
Head of the Roman college of priests responsible for religious law
Priestess of Apollo at Delphi who acted as the god's mouthpiece

flashcard_questions.q: What was the hiereus in ancient Greek religion?
flashcard_questions.a: A male priest serving a specific deity at a specific sanctuary, responsible for ritual and temple maintenance.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the primary duty of a Greek mantis?
flashcard_questions.a: To read divine omens — from bird flight, sacrificial fire and entrails — especially for generals before battle.

flashcard_questions.q: Where was the most famous oracle of ancient Greece located?
flashcard_questions.a: At Delphi, in the sanctuary of Apollo on the slopes of Mount Parnassus.

flashcard_questions.q: What title was given to the priestess who delivered Apollo's oracular responses at Delphi?
What was the famous ambiguous answer the Oracle gave to Croesus of Lydia?
flashcard_questions.a: That if he crossed the river Halys a great empire would be destroyed — his own, as it turned out.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the auspices in Roman religion?
flashcard_questions.a: Divine signs, especially from the behaviour and flight of birds, read by augures to establish divine approval.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the role of the pontifices in Rome?
flashcard_questions.a: To oversee religious law, the calendar and the correct performance of all state religious ceremonies.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Roman emperor took the title of Pontifex Maximus in 12 BC?
What was the primary duty of the Vestal Virgins?
flashcard_questions.a: To maintain the sacred fire in the Temple of Vesta in the Roman Forum.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the punishment for a Vestal Virgin who broke her vow of chastity?
Which Roman priestly officials were of Etruscan origin and specialised in reading the liver?

glossary_terms.definition: A Greek male priest (hiereus) or female priestess (hiereia) responsible for the maintenance of a temple and the performance of its rituals.
A Greek female priestess who served a deity, particularly a goddess, and performed the cult's rituals on behalf of the community.
A Greek prophet or seer who interpreted omens, dreams and signs from the gods, accompanying armies and advising leaders on the divine will.
The title given to the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who acted as the mouthpiece of the god, delivering oracular responses in a state of divine inspiration.
The college of Roman priests responsible for overseeing religious law, the calendar, public ceremonies and the correct performance of all state religious rites; headed by the Pontifex Maximus.
Roman priestly officials responsible for interpreting the will of the gods by observing the flight and behaviour of birds and other signs (auspices).
Divine signs interpreted by Roman augurs, especially from the behaviour and flight of birds, used to determine whether the gods approved of a proposed action.
